lines.text: The Hermetic Excerpts of Stobaeus

Translated from the Greek as the manuscripts of Stobaeus transmit it, with the excerpt and section numbering of Walter Scott’s edition (Oxford, 1924). The numbers in the margin give Scott’s excerpt and section.
Excerpt I · Hermes, from the discourse to Tat

To conceive God is difficult; to express him is impossible, even for one who is able to conceive him. For it is impossible to signify the incorporeal by means of body, and it is not possible to grasp the perfect by the imperfect, and it is hard for the eternal to keep company with the short-lived. For the one always is, while the other passes away; and the one is true, while the other is overshadowed by appearance. As far, then, as the weaker stands apart from the stronger and the lesser from the better, so far does the mortal stand apart from the divine.

And the interval that lies between them dims the vision of the beautiful. For bodies can be seen by the eyes, and visible things can be spoken of by the tongue; but that which is incorporeal and unmanifest and without shape, and has no substrate of matter, cannot be apprehended by our senses. I have in mind, Tat, I have in mind that which it is impossible to utter: this is God.
Excerpt II A · Hermes, from the discourses to Tat

Concerning truth, Tat, it is not possible for one who is a human being, an imperfect living being, composed of imperfect parts and with a tent made up of many alien bodies, to venture to speak; but what is possible or right, this I say: that truth exists only in the eternal bodies, of which

the very bodies too are true: fire that is fire itself alone and nothing else, earth that is earth itself and nothing else, air that is air itself, water that is water itself and nothing else. But our bodies are composed of all of these: for they have something of fire, and they have something of earth too, and of water and of air; and they are neither fire nor earth nor water nor air, nor anything true. And if our composition did not have truth to begin with, how could it either see truth or speak it? To think it is possible only if God wills.

All the things upon earth, then, Tat, are not truth, but imitations of truth; and not all of them, for these are but few. The rest are falsehood and error, Tat, and opinions born of appearance, put together like pictures.

But whenever the appearance has the influx from above, it becomes an imitation of truth; without the energy from above, it is left a falsehood. Just so the picture too shows the body in the painting, yet is not itself a body in the way that the thing seen appears to be; and it is seen to have eyes, yet it sees nothing, and it hears nothing at all; and the painting has all the other features too, but they are false, deceiving the sight of those who look at them, who suppose that they see truth, whereas the things are in truth false.

All those, then, who do not see falsehood see truth. If, therefore, we think or see each of these things as it is, we both think and see what is true; but if we do so contrary to what is, we shall neither think nor see anything true.
— There is truth, then, father, even on the earth.

— You are mistaken, my child, though not wide of the mark. Truth is in no way on the earth, Tat, nor can it come to be there; but that some among human beings should have thoughts about truth, those on whom God bestows the power of beholding God, this can come about.
Thus there is nothing true on the earth. I think it and I say it. All things are appearances and opinions. I think and say what is true.
— Then must we not call this very thing, thinking and saying what is true, truth?
— What then?
One must think and say the things that are, and there is nothing true upon the earth. This is what is true: that one knows nothing true here.

How indeed could it come to be, my child? For truth is the most perfect virtue, the unmixed good itself, that which is neither muddied by matter nor wrapped about by body: a good naked, radiant, unchangeable, august, unalterable. But the things here, my child, you see what they are: incapable of receiving this good, perishable, subject to affection, dissoluble, changeable, ever being altered, coming to be one out of another.

Things, then, that are not true even to themselves, how could they be true? For everything that is altered is falsehood, since it does not remain in what it is, but shifts about and displays to us one appearance after another.
— Is not even a human being true, father?

— In so far as he is a human being he is not true, my child. For the true is that which has its composition from itself alone and remains by itself such as it is; but a human being is composed of many things and does not remain by himself, but turns and changes from age to age and from form to form, and that while he is still in the tent. And many have failed to recognise their children when a short time had intervened, and children in turn their parents likewise.

Can that, then, which changes so as not to be recognised be true, Tat? Is it not, on the contrary, falsehood, since its changes come about in manifold appearances? But for your part, think of that alone which is eternal as something true. A human being, however, does not exist always; therefore he is not a true thing either, but a human being is a kind of appearance; and appearance would be the uttermost falsehood.
— Then are not even these eternal bodies true, father, since they change?

— Nothing, indeed, that is generated and changeable is true; but since they were made by the forefather, they may have received their matter as true. Yet these too have something false in their changing; for nothing that does not abide in itself is true.
— What, then, father, might one call true?

— The sun alone, which unlike all other things does not change but abides in itself, one might call truth. That is why he alone has been entrusted with the crafting of all things in the cosmos, ruling all things and making all things. Him I revere, and I worship his truth; after the one and first, I acknowledge him as craftsman.
— What, then, might one call the first truth, father?
— Him who is one and alone, Tat: he who is not of matter, he who is not in body; the colourless, the shapeless; the unchangeable, he who is not altered; he who always is.

But falsehood, my child, perishes. Destruction has laid hold of all things upon earth, and the providence of the true encompasses them and will encompass them; for without destruction not even generation can subsist. Upon every generation destruction follows, so that there may be generation again. For the things that come to be must necessarily come to be out of those that perish; and the things that come to be must necessarily perish, so that the generation of the things that are may not come to a standstill. Recognise this one as the first craftsman for the generation of the things that are. The things, then, that come to be out of destruction would be false, since they come to be now one thing and now another. For is it possible that the same things should come to be? And that which is not the same, how could it be true?

These things, then, must be called appearances, my child, if indeed we rightly call the human being an appearance of humanity, the child an appearance of a child, the youth an appearance of a youth, the grown man an appearance of a grown man, the old man an appearance of an old man; for the human being is not a human being, nor the child a child, nor the youth a youth, nor the grown man a grown man, nor the old man an old man;

but, changing, they belie both what they were before and what they are. Understand these things, however, in this way, my child: that even these false energies depend from above, from truth itself. And this being so, I say that falsehood is a work of truth.
Excerpt II B

I, my child, both for love of humankind and for piety towards God, am writing this down first of all. For there could be no piety more righteous than to understand the things that are and to acknowledge gratitude for them to him who made them; and this I shall go on doing without cease.
— What, then, father, should one do to pass one’s life well, if nothing here is true?

— Be pious, my child. And he who is pious in the highest degree will practise philosophy. For without philosophy it is impossible to be pious in the highest degree; but he who has learned what things are, and how they have been ordered, and by whom, and to what end, will be grateful for all things to the craftsman as to a good father, a kindly nurturer and a faithful guardian; and he who acknowledges gratitude will be pious.

And he who practises philosophy will learn both where truth is and what it is; and having learned, he will be more pious still. For never, my child, can a soul that is in a body, and has lightened itself for the apprehension of what is really good and true, slip back to the opposite; for a soul that has learned who its own forefather is is possessed by a mighty love, and by forgetfulness of all evils, and can no longer stand apart from the good.
This, my child, this is the end of piety; and when you arrive at it you will both live well and die happily, since your soul will not be ignorant of where it must wing its way upward.

For this alone, my child, is the road to truth, which our ancestors also travelled, and having travelled it they attained the good. August is this road, and smooth, but hard for a soul to travel while it is in a body.

For first it must make war upon itself, and bring about a great division, and the greater number must be overcome by the one part. For the conflict is of one against two, the one fleeing and the others dragging it downward; and there arises much strife and battle of these with one another, the one wishing to flee and the others striving to hold it fast.

But the victory of the two sides is not alike; for the one presses towards the good, while the others make their home among evils; and the one longs to be set free, while the others love their slavery. And if the two parts are defeated, they remain bereft of themselves and of their ruler; but if the one is worsted, it is led and carried off by the two, punished by its way of life here.

This, my child, is the guide on the road that leads there; for you must, my child, first leave the body behind before the end, and win the victory in the life of contest, and, having won it, so ascend.
Excerpt III

For the energies, Tat, though they are themselves incorporeal, are in bodies and work through bodies. Therefore, Tat, in so far as they are incorporeal, you say that they are also immortal; but in so far as they cannot work apart from bodies, I say that they are always in a body.
For the things that have come to be in relation to something or for the sake of something, being subject to providence and necessity,
cannot ever remain idle, without their proper energy. For that which is will always be; for this is both its body and its life.

From this argument it follows also that bodies always exist. Hence I say that embodiment itself is an eternal energy. For if earthly bodies are dissoluble, and yet there must be bodies, since these are the places and instruments of the energies, and the energies are immortal, and the immortal always is, then the making of bodies too is an energy, if indeed it always is.

They attend upon the soul, though they do not arrive all at once; rather, some of them are at work from the moment the human being is born, being concerned, along with the soul, with the irrational parts, while the purer energies, upon the change from quiescence, work together with the rational part of the soul.

These energies are dependent on bodies. And from the divine bodies there come into mortal ones these body-making energies, and each of them works either upon the body or upon the soul. And indeed they consort with the soul itself apart from body. Energies exist always, but the soul is not always in a mortal body; for it can exist apart from the body, whereas the energies cannot exist apart from bodies.
This, my child, is a sacred discourse.
A body cannot hold together without soul, but it can exist.
— What do you mean by this, father?

— Think of it thus, Tat. When the soul has been separated from the body, the body itself persists. But this body, during the time of its persistence, is worked upon by energy, being dissolved and passing out of sight. And the body cannot undergo these things without an energy. The energy itself, therefore, persists in the body when the soul has been separated.

This, then, is the difference between an immortal body and a mortal one: that the immortal is composed of a single matter, and the other is not; and that the one acts, while the other is acted upon. For everything that exerts energy is master, and that which is worked upon by energy is mastered. And that which is master, being commanding and free, leads; while the other, a slave, is carried along.

The energies work not only upon ensouled bodies but upon the soulless as well, wood and stones and the other things of that kind, making them grow and bear fruit and ripen, and destroying and melting and rotting and crumbling them, and working all such effects as soulless bodies are capable of undergoing. For energy, my child, is the name given to just this: whatever it is that is coming to be.

And there must always be many things coming to be, or rather all things. For the cosmos is never bereft of any of the things that are, but, ever borne along, it conceives within itself the things that are, which will never be free of its destruction.
Let every energy, then, be thought of as being always immortal, whichever it may be that is in a body of whatever kind.

Of the energies, some belong to the divine bodies and others to the perishable; and some are universal, others specific. And some belong to the kinds, others to each single one of the parts. Divine, then, are those that work upon their own bodies; and these are also perfect, as working upon perfect bodies. Partial are those that work through each single kind of living beings; and specific, those that work upon each particular one of the things that are.

This argument, my child, leads to the conclusion that all things are full of energies. For if the energies must be in bodies, and there are many bodies in the cosmos, I say that the energies are more numerous than the bodies. For in a single body there is often a first and a second and a third, not counting the universal ones that attend it; for I call universal energies those that are truly bodily, and that come about through the sensations and the movements; for without these energies the body cannot hold together. And there are other, specific energies belonging to the souls of human beings, through arts and sciences and pursuits and works.
For sensations too attend upon the energies; or rather, sensations are the finished effects of the energies.

Understand, then, my child, the difference between energy and sensation. For energy is sent from above; but sensation, being in the body and having its essence from it, receives the energy and makes it manifest, as though it had given it a body. Therefore I say that sensations are both bodily and mortal, subsisting just as long as the body does; for sensations are born together with the body and die together with it.

But the immortal bodies themselves have no sensation, as being composed of an essence of such a kind. For sensation, being bodily, is of nothing else whatever than the evil or the good that is added to the body, or again that which departs from it; but to the eternal bodies nothing is either added or taken away; therefore sensation does not arise in them.
— Does sensation, then, sense in every body?
— In every one, my child; and energies work in all.
— Even in soulless things, father?

— Even in soulless things, my child. But there are differences among sensations: those of rational beings come about with reason; those of irrational beings are bodily only; and those of soulless things

are sensations indeed, but passive ones, arising only in respect of growth and in respect of diminution. Affection and sensation depend from a single summit, and are gathered into the same thing, and that by the energies.

In ensouled living beings there are two other energies, which attend upon the sensations and the affections: grief and joy. Without these it is impossible for an ensouled living being, and above all a rational one, to have sensation; hence I say that these are distinct forms of the affections, which hold the greater sway over the rational living beings. The energies work, and the sensations bring the energies to light.

And these, being bodily, are stirred up by the irrational parts of the soul; hence I say that both are harmful. For rejoicing, which furnishes sensation together with pleasure, proves straightway the cause of many evils to the one who experiences it; and grief brings on sufferings and pains that are more severe. Therefore both alike would with good reason be harmful.
— Would the sensation of soul and of body be the same, father?
— How do you conceive sensation of soul, my child? Is not the soul incorporeal, and sensation a body?
— * * * would be, father, the sensation that is in fact in a body.

— If we posit it as incorporeal, my child, we shall be declaring it to be like the soul or the energies; for these, we say, though incorporeal, are in bodies. But sensation is neither an energy nor a soul, nor any other incorporeal thing besides those already mentioned; it would not, therefore, be incorporeal. And if it is not incorporeal, it would be a body. For of the things that are, some must be bodies and the others incorporeal.
Excerpt IV A
For we said in the General Discourses that some movements are caused by the energies and others by the bodies.

And we say that the soul has come to be out of a certain essence, not out of matter, being incorporeal, that essence itself being incorporeal as well. For everything that has come to be must necessarily have come to be out of something.

For all things, then, in which destruction follows upon generation, two movements must necessarily attend: that of the soul, by which they are moved, and that of the body, by which they grow and waste away, and furthermore, once broken up, are dissolved. This I define as the movement of perishable bodies.

But the soul is ever-moving, because it is always in movement of itself and works movement in other things. According to this reasoning, then, every soul is immortal, in so far as it is ever-moving, having as its movement its own energy.
The forms of souls are: divine, human, irrational. The divine soul, then, is the energy of its divine body; for it moves within that body, and moves it.

For when it has been released from mortal living beings, separated from its own irrational parts, it goes forth into the divine body and, being ever-moving, moves within it, carried round together with the universe.

The human soul has also something of the divine, but there are joined to it the irrational parts as well, desire and anger. These too are immortal, inasmuch as they too are in fact energies, but energies of mortal bodies. Hence they are far removed from the divine part of the soul while the soul is in the divine body; but when this part enters a mortal body, those also grow upon it, and by their presence it becomes in every case a human soul.
The soul of irrational beings is composed of anger and desire. That is why these living beings were called irrational, by privation of the rational part of the soul.

As a fourth, think of the soul of soulless things, which, being outside the bodies, works upon them by moving them. This would be the soul that moves in the divine body and moves these things as it were in passing.
Excerpt IV B

— You have demonstrated these things rightly, father; but teach me this further point. For you said somewhere that science and art are energies of the rational part. But now you say that the irrational living beings are irrational, and are so called, by privation of the rational part; clearly, by this reasoning, the irrational living beings must have no share in science or in art, because they have been deprived of the rational part.
— Necessarily so, my child.

— How is it, then, father, that we see some of the irrational creatures making use of science and art: the ants, for instance, storing up their food against the winter, and the creatures of the air likewise putting together nests for themselves, and the four-footed beasts knowing their own lairs?

— These things, my child, they do not by science nor by art, but by nature. For science and art are things that are taught; but none of the irrational creatures is taught any of these things. And the things that come about by nature come about by a universal energy; whereas the things that come about by science and art accrue to those who know, not to all; what comes about for all is worked by nature.

For example, human beings look upward; but not all human beings are musicians, nor are all archers or hunters, and so with all the rest; rather, some of them have learned some one thing, science and art being at work.

In the same way, if some of the ants did this and others did not, you would be right in saying that they do this very thing by science and gather their food by art; but if all alike are led to this by nature, even against their will, it is clear that they do not do this by science or by art.
Excerpt V

And the lord and craftsman of all the eternal bodies, Tat, having made them once, made no more, nor does he make now; for having handed these over to themselves and united them with one another, he let them go on their course, lacking nothing, as being eternal. And if they have need of anything, it is of one another that they will have need, but of no supply brought in from outside, since they are immortal; for it was necessary that the bodies which came into being by him should also have a nature of such a kind.

But our own craftsman, being in a body, made us, and makes us always and will make us, bodies dissoluble and mortal. For it was not lawful for him to imitate his own craftsman, and besides it was impossible; for the one made from the first essence, which is incorporeal, whereas the other made us from the embodiment that comes into being.

With good reason, then, according to right reason, those bodies, as having come into being from incorporeal essence, are immortal; whereas ours are dissoluble and mortal, since our matter is composed of bodies.

Hence they are weak, and in need of much assistance. For how could the bond of our bodies have held out even for the briefest time, if it did not have some nourishment coming in from the like elements, which built our bodies up afresh every day? For indeed an inflow of earth and water and fire and air comes to us, which, by renewing our bodies, holds the tent together.

And so we are also too weak for movements, unable to bear the movements of even a single day. For know well, my child, that if our bodies did not rest in the nights, we should not have held out for one day. Hence the craftsman, being good and knowing all things beforehand, made sleep for the continuance of the living being, the greatest remedy for the weariness of movement, and he assigned a time to each in equal measure, or rather a longer one to rest.

Understand, my child, that the energy of sleep is very great, the opposite of that of the soul, and no less than it. For just as the soul is an energy of movement, in the same way bodies too cannot live without sleep; for it is a slackening and release of the fastenings of the limbs.

And it works from within, making into body the matter that has come in, and distributing to each part what is proper to it: water to the blood, earth to bones and marrow, air to the sinews and veins, fire to the sight. That is why the body takes the utmost pleasure in sleep, since sleep works this pleasure.
Excerpt VI · Hermes, from the discourses to Tat
Since in the earlier General Discourses you promised to explain to me about the thirty-six decans, explain to me now about them and about their energy.
— I grudge you nothing, Tat; and this would be the most authoritative discourse of all, and the crowning one. Understand it, then, in this way.
We spoke to you about the zodiacal circle, that is, the circle that bears the living figures, and about the five planets and the sun and the moon and the circle of each of these.
— You did, Trismegistus.
— In the same way I want you to think also about the thirty-six decans, remembering those things, so that the account of these too may be easy for you to grasp.
— I remember, father.
— We say, I suppose, my child, that there is a body which encompasses all things. Conceive of this too, then, as a kind of circular figure; for so it is with the universe.
— I conceive such a figure, just as you say, father.

— And beneath the circle of this body, understand, these thirty-six decans have been stationed, midway between the circle of the universe and that of the zodiac, dividing the two circles from one another, and as it were bearing up the former and marking the bounds of the zodiac,

borne along with the planets; and that they have a power equal to the motion of the universe, in alternation with the seven; and that they hold back the encompassing body, for left to itself it would be at the extreme in its motion, in what it undergoes, but hasten on the seven other circles, because these move with a slower motion than the circle of the universe; just as, indeed, it is necessary that they should be moved, and the circle of the universe as well.

Let us understand, then, that they stand around the spheres of the seven and the whole circle, or rather around all the things in the cosmos, as their guardians, so to speak, holding all things together, the whole of them, and preserving the good order of all.
— So indeed I understand it, father, from what you say.

— Understand further, Tat, that they are also unaffected by what the other stars undergo. For they neither come to a standstill, checked in their course, nor move backward, being hindered, nor again are they covered over by the light of the sun, all of which the other stars undergo; but being free, and above all things, as exact guardians and overseers of the universe they compass the universe in a night and a day.
— Do these too, then, father, have an energy that bears upon us?
— The greatest, my child. For if they work upon those, how should they not work upon us too, both upon each one singly and upon all in common?

Thus, my child, the energy at work in all the things that happen universally comes from these; for example, and mark what I say, the overthrow of kings, the uprisings of cities, famines, plagues, the ebbing of the sea, earthquakes: none of these, my child, comes about without the energy of these.

And consider this further besides. If these preside over those, and we in turn are under the seven, do you not understand that some energy of theirs reaches us as well, whether from themselves or through those?
— What, father, would be the form of their body?

— These, then, the many call daemons; for the daemons are not some distinct kind of their own, neither having other bodies made of some matter of their own nor being moved by soul as we are, but they are energies of these thirty-six gods.
And further, besides this, consider, Tat, a working of theirs: that they also sow upon the earth what people call tanai, some of them salutary, others most destructive.

Further, borne along in heaven as stars, they beget for themselves subordinate ministers, whom they keep as servants and soldiers. And these, mingled together by them, are borne along suspended in the aether, filling up its region, so that no place above may be empty of stars; they join in ordering the universe, having an energy of their own, yet one subordinated to the energy of the thirty-six. From them come also the destructions, region by region, of the other ensouled living beings, and the swarming of the creatures that ravage the crops.

Beneath these is the so-called Bear, at the middle of the zodiac, composed of seven stars, with another, its counterpart, overhead. Its energy is like that of an axle: it nowhere sets nor rises, but remains in the same place, turning about the same point, and it works the revolution of the circle that bears the living figures, handing this universe over from night to day and from day to night.
After these there is another choir of stars, which we have not deemed worthy of names; but those who come after us, imitating us, will themselves give names to these too.

Below the moon there are other stars, perishable, inert, formed for a short time, exhaled from the earth itself into the air above the earth, which we ourselves see dissolving. They have a nature like that of the useless creatures upon earth, which come into being for no other end than only to perish, such as the race of flies and of fleas and of worms and of the others like them. For just as those, Tat, are useful neither to us nor to the cosmos, but on the contrary distress us with their annoyance, being by-products of nature and having their generation as something superfluous, in the same way also the stars exhaled from the earth do not attain the upper region, for they cannot, since they rise from below; but having much that is heavy in them, and being dragged down by their own matter, they are quickly dispersed, and once dissolved they fall back to earth, having effected nothing except merely to trouble the air above the earth.

There is another kind, Tat, that of the so-called comets, which appear at their due season and after a short time become invisible again, neither rising nor setting nor being dissolved; they become the manifest messengers and heralds of universal outcomes that are about to be. These have their place beneath the circle of the sun. Whenever, then, something is about to befall the cosmos, these appear; and having appeared for a few days, they go back beneath the circle of the sun and remain unseen, some having appeared in the east, others in the north, others in the west, others in the south. We have named them seers. Such is the nature of the stars.

Stars (asteres) differ from constellations (astra). For stars are those that hang suspended in heaven, whereas constellations are those that lie fixed in the body of heaven and are borne along together in heaven; from among these we have named twelve the signs of the zodiac.
He who is not ignorant of these things can understand God exactly, and, if one must make bold to say it, can even become an eyewitness and behold him, and having beheld him become blessed.
— Blessed in very truth, father, is he who has beheld him.

— But it is impossible, my child, for one who is in a body to attain this good fortune; one must train one’s soul beforehand here, so that when it has come there, where it is permitted to behold him, it may not miss the way.
But all those human beings who are lovers of the body could never behold the vision of the beautiful and good. For what a beauty it is, my child, that which has neither figure nor colour nor body!
— But could there be anything beautiful apart from these, father?
— God alone, my child, or rather that which is something greater than the name of God.
Excerpt VII · Hermes

For a very great daemon has been appointed, my child, who revolves in the midst of the universe and surveys all that is done on earth by human beings. Just as providence and necessity have been set over the divine order, in the same way Justice has been set over human beings, working the same effects as they do.

For the former holds sway over the order of the things that are, inasmuch as they are divine and neither wish to sin nor are able to; for it is impossible for the divine to go astray, and from this it follows that it is also free of sin. But Justice has been appointed as the punisher of those who sin upon earth.

For as to the race of human beings, since it is mortal and composed of evil matter, slipping befalls it, and most of all those in whom the power of seeing God is not present; and over these most of all Justice prevails. And it is subject to fate because of the energies of its birth, but to Justice because of the sins committed in life.
Excerpt VIII · Hermes, from the discourses to Tat
You have told me everything rightly, father. But remind me further what the things are that are according to providence, and likewise what are according to necessity, and according to fate.

— I said, Tat, that there are in us three kinds of incorporeal things. One of them is something intelligible. This, then, is without colour, without figure, incorporeal, coming from the first and intelligible essence itself.

There are also in us configurations opposed to this; this receives them. At any rate, that which is moved by the intelligible essence in relation to a certain reason, once it has been received, changes at once into another form of movement; and this is an image of the thought of the craftsman.

The third kind of incorporeal things is that which is an accident attending bodies: place, time, movement, figure, surface, magnitude, form. And of these there are two different sorts; for some of them are qualities in the strict sense, while others belong to the body. The qualities in the strict sense are figure, colour, form, place, time, movement; while those proper to the body are the figure that has been figured and the colour that has been coloured, and there is also the shape that has been shaped, and the surface, and the magnitude. These have no share in those.

Now the intelligible essence, when it has come to be with God, has authority over itself, and over the preserving of another while it preserves itself; and then, being itself, it is not under necessity. But when it has been left behind by God, it chooses the bodily nature, and its choice is according to providence, and by this it comes to belong to the cosmos.
And everything irrational is moved in relation to a certain reason.

And reason is according to providence, the irrational according to necessity, and the accidents attending the body according to fate. And this is the account of the things that are according to providence and necessity and according to fate.

Cronus announced that he was already father of Justice and Necessity. Zeus said: ‘So that the tribe that is to be may not utterly perish by wars, I have already begotten for them Fortune and Hope and Peace.’ Ares said that he was already father of Struggle and Wrath and Strife. Aphrodite did not delay, but said: ‘And I, master, will yoke to them Longing and Pleasure and Laughter, so that the kindred souls, enduring a most harsh condemnation, may not be punished beyond measure.’ He was delighted the more, my child, when Aphrodite said this.

‘And I’, said Hermes, ‘will both make the nature of human beings and set beside them wisdom and temperance and persuasion and truth; and I will not cease to keep company with Invention, but will also benefit for ever the mortal life of the human beings born under my signs of the zodiac—for the signs which the father and craftsman dedicated to me are endowed with understanding and intelligence—and the more so when the movement of the stars that lies over them has the natural energy of each one in concord with it.’ God, the master of the cosmos, rejoiced on hearing this, and commanded that the tribe of human beings come into being.

And I, says Hermes, was seeking for matter, what I ought to use. And I called upon the monarch; and he commanded the souls to give the remainder of the blend. And taking it I found it altogether dry. So I used far more water than was needed in the mixing, so as to make the composition of the matter fresh again, so that the thing moulded should be altogether slack and weak and powerless, lest in addition to being discerning it should also be filled with power. I moulded it; and it was beautiful, and I was delighted as I looked upon my work. And from below I called upon the monarch to behold it; and he both saw it and rejoiced, and commanded the souls to be embodied.
And they then for the first time grew sullen, on learning that they were condemned; and so I marvelled also at the words of the souls.

Give heed, my child Horus, for you are hearing a hidden doctrine, which the forefather Kamephis came to hear from Hermes, the recorder of all deeds, and I from Kamephis, elder than all, when he honoured me also with the perfect black; and now you yourself hear it from me.

For when, wondrous child of great renown, they were about to be shut up in the bodies, some of them merely wailed and groaned; and it was in the very way in which, among the wild beasts that have come into being, the free ones, when by the designs of wicked men they are torn away as slaves from their accustomed and beloved wilderness, fight and rebel and are not of one mind with those who have mastered them, but will even, if they chance to prevail, hand over to death those who lay hands on them. And others hissed in the manner of ancient asps.

And another, having shrieked shrilly, and wept much before she spoke, and many times turning upward and downward her eyes, such as they were, said: ‘O heaven, origin of our birth, and aether and air, and hands and holy breath of God the monarch, and you brilliant stars, eyes of the gods, and unwearied light of sun and moon, nurslings together with our origin: torn away from all of you we suffer wretchedly. And the more so, that from things great and bright, and from the holy effusion that lies around and the neighbouring vault, and from the blessed commonwealth with gods, we shall be shut up like this in dishonoured and lowly tents.

‘What so unseemly thing has been done by us wretches? What is deserving of these punishments? What sins await us in our misery! What things we shall do because of our evil hopes, in order to supply the needs of the watery and swiftly dissolving body!

‘Eyes will afford but scant room to souls that are no longer God’s; and seeing heaven, our own forefather, as something altogether small through the moisture within them and their little circles, we shall groan for ever. And there will be times when we shall not see at all; whence Orpheus says: “By what is bright we see; with our eyes we behold nothing.” For, wretches that we are, we have been condemned, and sight has not been granted us outright, because seeing was not given us apart from the light. These, then, are places, and eyes no longer. And how miserably shall we bear to hear our kindred breaths blowing in the air, because we do not breathe together with them! For a home, in place of this lofty cosmos, the small bulk of a heart awaits us.

‘And he who sets us free for ever will make an end of our grieving over the things from which, and into what, we have come down. Master and father and maker, if you have so quickly ceased to care for your own works, appoint for us some limits. Deem us worthy still of words, however few, while we are yet able to see through the whole of the cosmos in its full brightness.’

The souls, my child Horus, gained their request when they had said this; for the monarch too was at hand, and, taking his seat upon the throne of truth, he spoke as follows to those who had made their petition:
The words of God.

‘Love and Necessity, souls, shall be your masters; for these, after me, are the masters and marshals of all things. And you souls, as many as serve my ageless sceptred rule, know that so long as you were without sin you dwelt in the regions of heaven; but if any blame shall come near any one of you, you too shall be condemned to dwell in mortal entrails, the place allotted to you.

‘And if the charges against you are moderate, you shall leave behind the perishable bond of the flesh and once more, without a groan, greet your own heaven; but if you prove to be the doers of any greater sins, then, coming forth from your moulded frames without the fitting end, you shall dwell no longer in heaven, nor yet in the bodies of human beings, but shall thereafter go on wandering from one irrational animal to another.’

Having said this, my child Horus, he bestowed spirits upon them all, and spoke again: ‘Nor was it at random and as chance would have it that the changes of your state were laid down as law: as they will be for the worse if you do anything unseemly, so they will be for the better if you resolve on anything worthy of your own origin; for I myself, and no other, shall be the watcher and overseer. Recognise, then, that it is on account of the things you did before that you undergo this punishment, embodiment.

‘The difference in your rebirth, then, will be, as I said, the difference of bodies, and dissolution will be a benefit and the happiness of former times; but your understanding will be blinded, if you see fit to do anything unworthy of me, so that you think the contrary, and endure the punishment as though it were a benefit, and the change to better things as a dishonour and an outrage. But the more just among you, who look to receive the change into the divine,

‘on passing into human beings, will be just kings, genuine philosophers, founders and lawgivers, the true seers, genuine root-cutters, most excellent prophets of the gods, skilled musicians, intelligent astronomers, unerring augurs, exact sacrificers, and all who are of worth in any of the things fair and good. Passing into birds, they will be eagles, because these will neither drive off with their cries any of their own kind nor feast upon them, nor, moreover, will any other animal in their neighbourhood be left free to wrong one weaker than itself; for the nature of eagles, most just as it is, will exact vengeance. Passing into four-footed beasts, they will be lions; for the animal is strong, and has received a nature that is in a manner sleepless, and in a perishable body it exercises itself in the immortal nature; for they neither tire nor sleep. Passing into creeping things, they will be great serpents, because the animal is powerful and long-lived, and harmless too, and so friendly to humankind that some are even tamed; and it has no venom, and it grows young again even when it has grown old, as does the nature of the gods. And among swimming things, dolphins; for these will feel compassion even for those who fall into the open sea, and whoever still has breath they will carry through to land, while those who have died they never touch at all, although the race of water-dwellers is the most voracious of all.’
Having said so much, God becomes invisible mind.

When these things had so come to pass, my child Horus, a most mighty spirit rises up from the earth, not to be comprehended in the compass of its body, and surpassing in the power of its understanding. This spirit, although it knew the things about which it was inquiring—it wore a body after the pattern of a man, one both comely and of solemn bearing, yet savage beyond measure and full of terror—this spirit, the moment it beheld the souls entering into the moulded frames, said: ‘What are these called, Hermes, recorder of the gods?’

And when he said ‘Human beings’, it said: ‘Hermes, it is a daring work to have made the human being, a creature prying with his eyes and of chattering tongue, only too apt to listen even to what is none of his concern, greedy in his sense of smell, and bound to misuse to the utmost the grasping power of his touch. Have you resolved, author of generation, to leave him free of care, this one who is going to look daringly upon the fair mysteries of nature? Do you mean to let him go without grief, this one who will send forth his own designs even to the things beyond the earth?

‘Human beings will dig up the roots of plants and will test the quality of their juices; they will scrutinise the natures of stones; and they will cut open down the middle those of the animals that are irrational—and not these only, but themselves as well, wishing to find out how they came to be. They stretch out daring hands even as far as the sea, and, felling the self-grown forests, they ferry one another across even to the lands beyond, in search also of what nature lies deeper within the sacred inner shrines. They will pursue things right up to the heights, wishing to observe what movement, then, is established there. Even this is moderate. For nothing is left any longer but the uttermost region of the earth; yet of these places too they will, by sheer willing, search out the uttermost night.

‘Are these, then, to have no hindrance, but to be initiated into the good of truth and, not constrained by the harsh goads of fear, to luxuriate in a life free of care? Will not the human being then arm himself with a prying daring that reaches even to heaven? Will not these stretch out their souls, free of care, even to the elements? Teach them, therefore, to be in love with planning something, so that they may also have the hardship of failure to fear, so that they may be tamed by the bite of grief when they fail of the things they hoped for. Let the prying of their souls be cheated of its due by desires and fears and griefs and deceiving hopes. Let loves in close succession prey upon their souls, and manifold hopes, and desires that at one time attain their object and at another miss it, so that even the sweetness of success may be for them a bait drawing them on to contend with more complete evils. Let fever weigh upon them, so that, losing heart, they may chastise their desire.’

Are you grieved, my child Horus, as your mother expounds these things to you? Do you not marvel, are you not struck with dismay, at how the wretched human being was weighed down? Hear something more terrible still.

Hermes was pleased as Momus said these things; for what was said was spoken in a manner congenial to him. And he set about doing all just as Momus had said, saying: ‘But, Momus, the nature of the divine spirit, that of the encompassing expanse, shall no longer lie idle. For the master of all things has declared that I am to be steward and to exercise providence. The keen-sighted goddess Adrasteia, then, shall be overseer of the things of earth, of the whole. And I will devise a hidden instrument, bound to an unerring and inviolable vision, to which all things on earth will of necessity be enslaved, from birth to final destruction, an instrument that holds fixed the outcome of all that is brought to pass; and all other things on earth too will obey this instrument.’ These things I said to Momus, said Hermes, and already the instrument was in motion.
And when these things had come to pass, and the souls had been embodied, and he himself had won praise for what had been done,

the monarch again convened an assembly of the gods in full session. And the gods came, and again he himself spoke thus, saying: ‘Gods, all you who have been given the highest nature, a nature that is imperishable too, you to whom it has fallen by lot to govern the great aeon for ever, you for whom all things, handing themselves on in turn one to another, will never grow weary: how long shall we be masters of this sovereignty that goes unrecognised? How long shall these things remain unbeheld by sun and moon? Let each of us beget for his own part. Let us by our power wipe away this structure that still lies idle. Let it seem to those born hereafter an incredible tale that there was chaos. Set your hands to great works, and I myself will be the first to begin.’ He spoke, and at once the still-black unity was parted in cosmic order; and

heaven appeared above, arrayed with all its own mysteries; the earth, still quaking, grew firm when the sun shone out, and appeared with all the fair things arrayed about her. For to God even the things that mortals deem mean are fair, because they were made to serve the laws of God. And God rejoiced, seeing his works now in motion.

And having filled his hands, which are of equal measure with the encompassing expanse, with the things that were to hand from nature, and having tightly clenched his fists, he said: ‘Take, holy earth, take, all-honoured one, you who are to be the mother of all things, and think yourself from now on to fall short in nothing.’ God spoke, and opening his hands—such hands as a god must have—he let everything go into the structure of the things that are.

And at the beginning nothing whatever was known. For the souls, newly imprisoned and unable to bear their dishonour, vied with the gods in heaven; holding fast to their own noble birth and laying claim to it, on the ground that they too had had the same craftsman, they rose in revolt; and, using the lesser human beings as their instruments, they made them set upon one another, and range themselves against one another, and make war on each other. And so strength had great power over weakness, so that the strong both burned and slaughtered the powerless, and flung them down upon the holy places, some alive and others even dead, down into the inner shrines;

until the elements, in their indignation, resolved to petition God the monarch concerning the savage way of life of human beings; and when the evil had now grown great, the elements approached the God who had made them and, by way of complaint, used words such as these.

And indeed fire had leave to speak first, and said: ‘Master and craftsman of this new cosmos, name hidden among the gods and revered until now by all human beings, how long, O daemon, is it your purpose to leave the life of mortals godless?

‘Rise now upon the cosmos that seeks your answer, and initiate the savagery of life into peace. Bestow laws upon life. Bestow oracles upon the night. Fill all things with fair hopes. Let human beings fear the vengeance that comes from the gods, and no one will sin. If they receive wages that match their sins, the rest will guard against doing wrong. They will fear oaths, and not one will any longer harbour an unholy thought. Let them learn to give thanks for the benefits they have received, so that I, the fire, rejoicing as I do my service at libations and at sacrifices, may send up to you fragrant vapours from the hearth. For until now, master, I rage, and by the godless daring of the human beings who have come into being I am forced to melt flesh. And they do not let me remain in that for which I was born, debasing in unfitting fashion what is imperishable.’

And air said: ‘I too am made turbid, master, and by the exhalation from dead bodies I am full of disease and no longer wholesome; and I look down from above upon such things as it is not lawful to see.’

Water next, my great-souled child, had leave to speak, and spoke thus: ‘Father and wondrous maker of all things, self-begotten daemon and maker of the nature that through you begets all things, now at last, O daemon, command that the streams of the rivers be always pure; for rivers and seas either wash clean those who have slain or receive those who have been slain.’

Earth stood by next in deep sorrow; and—I will give her her place in the order of the speeches, my child of great renown—she began to speak thus: ‘King, and ruler and master of the heavenly vaults, leader and father of us the elements who stand before you, from which all things have the beginning of their increase and of their diminution, and into which, coming to their close once more, they have of necessity the end that is owed: a troop without reason and without god, O most honoured one, presses upon me from humankind. And I hold the nature of all things as well; for I myself, as you commanded, both bear all things and receive what has been slain. But now I am dishonoured.

‘You who are over all things, your earthly cosmos, full as it is, has no god. For, having nothing to fear, they transgress in everything; and upon my sinews, lord, they fall down by every wicked art, and I am drenched through and through with the juices of rotting bodies.

‘Hence, lord, I am forced to hold even the unworthy; I wish to hold, along with all that I bear, a god as well. Bestow upon the earth, if not yourself—for I cannot endure to hold you—some holy effluence of yourself. Make the earth over into something more honoured than the other elements; for she alone of the things that come from you has the right to make a boast, as the one who furnishes all things.’

So much the elements said; and God, filling all things with a holy voice as he spoke, said: ‘Go your ways, holy children, worthy of a great father, and in no way attempt to make any upheaval, nor leave my whole cosmos idle for want of the service that comes from you. For there is now among you another effluence of my nature, who shall indeed be a holy watcher of the deeds that are done, and of the living a judge who cannot be outwitted, and of those beneath the earth a ruler not only fearsome but avenging as well; and each human being shall be attended, down through his line, by the wage he deserves.’
And so the elements ceased from their petition at the master’s command, and held their peace; and each of them exercised rule and mastery in its own province.
— And thereupon Horus said: Mother, how then did the earth have the good fortune to receive the effluence of God?

— And Isis said: I decline to recount a birth; for it is not permitted to tell the origin of your begetting, mighty Horus, lest the birth of immortal gods should ever hereafter reach humankind; save only this, that God the monarch, the cosmos-maker and craftsman of all things, bestowed upon the earth for a little while your father, the most great Osiris, and the most great goddess Isis, that they might become helpers to the cosmos, which was in need of all things.

It was they who filled life with life. They put an end to the savagery of mutual slaughter. They themselves consecrated precincts and sacrifices to the ancestral gods; they bestowed on mortals laws and food and shelter.

‘They’, says Hermes, ‘will come to know all the hidden things of my writings and will distinguish them; and some they will keep to themselves, but those which bear upon benefits for mortals they will engrave on stelae and obelisks.’
They were the first to institute courts of law, and they filled all things with good order and justice.

They, becoming the founders of the pledged right hand and of good faith, also brought into life the most great god, Oath. They taught how those who have ceased to live should be wrapped for burial as is right.

They, having sought the cause of death, came to know that the breath from without is prone to return into the moulded frames of human beings, and that, if ever it fails to come, it brings about a swoon that admits of no recovery.
They, having learned from Hermes that the encompassing expanse was filled with daemons, engraved it on hidden stelae.
They alone, having learned from Hermes the hidden ordinances of God, became for human beings the introducers of all arts and sciences and pursuits, and their lawgivers.

They, having learned from Hermes that the things below were appointed by the craftsman to be in sympathy with the things above, set up on earth the sacred rites that answer, as on a plumb-line, to the mysteries in heaven.

They, recognising the perishableness of bodies, devised the perfection in all things of the prophets, so that the prophet who is to lay his hands upon the gods should never be ignorant of anything that is, in order that by philosophy and magic he may nourish the soul, and by medicine preserve the body whenever it suffers anything.

Having done all these things, my child, Osiris and I, seeing the cosmos filled to the full, were thereafter claimed back by those who dwell in heaven. But it was not possible to ascend before we had called upon the monarch, so that the encompassing expanse too might become full of this doctrine, and we ourselves, readily received, might have a prosperous ascent. For God delights in hymns.
— Mother, said Horus, grant to me also the knowledge of the hymn, that I may not be unlearned.
— And Isis said: Give heed, my child.
