But you, my great-souled child, if you wish for anything further, ask.
— And Horus said: Most honoured mother, I wish to know how kingly souls come to be.

— And Isis said: The difference that arises, my child Horus, in the case of kingly souls is something of this kind. For there are four places in the universe, which fall under an inviolable law and governance: heaven, the aether, the air, and the most holy earth. Above, my child, in heaven dwell gods, over whom, as over all the rest as well, the craftsman of all things rules; in the aether dwell stars, over whom rules the great luminary, the sun; in the air, souls alone, over whom the moon rules; and upon the earth, human beings and the other living beings, over whom rules he who is king at the time; for the gods, my child, beget kings worthy of the sovereignty on earth.

And the rulers are effluences of the king, and whichever of them is nearer to him is also more kingly than the others. For the sun, inasmuch as it is nearer to God, is greater and more powerful than the moon; and the moon holds second place to it both in rank and in power.

And the king is the last of the other gods, but the first of human beings. So long as he is upon earth he is removed from true divinity, yet he has something exceptional beyond human beings, which is like God; for the soul sent down into him is from that region which lies above those from which souls are sent down into other human beings.

Souls are sent down from there to reign, my child, for these two reasons. Those that have run the course of their own lifetime nobly and blamelessly, and are about to be made gods, are sent so that in reigning also they may be trained beforehand for the authority of the gods; and those that are already in some sort divine, and have in some small matter transgressed the divinely inspired rule, are sent so that they may not undergo punishment in their embodiment through disrepute and through their nature, and may suffer nothing like the other souls on being embodied, but may possess, even when bound, that which they possessed when unbound.

The differences, however, that arise in the characters of those who reign are not determined by the nature of the soul, for all are divine, but by that of the angels and daemons who attended its descent as a bodyguard. For souls of such a kind, coming down for such ends, do not come down without escort and bodyguard; for the justice on high knows how to assign to each its due, even though they are thrust out of the land of happiness.

When, therefore, the angels and daemons who bring the soul down are warlike, my child Horus, the soul has to keep fast hold of their cast of mind, having forgotten its own works and remembering only those, down to the last, that have accrued to it from its sacred escort; when they are peaceable, then the soul too makes its own course one of peace; when they are judicial, then it too gives judgement; when they are musical, then it too sings; when they are lovers of truth, then it too philosophises. For these souls, as by necessity, keep fast hold of the cast of mind of those who bring them down; for they fall into humanity having forgotten their own nature, and the more so as they have withdrawn far from it, but remembering the disposition of those who shut them in.
— Well have you told me everything, mother, said Horus; but how noble souls come to be you have not yet related to me.
How noble souls come to be.

— Just as upon earth, my child Horus, there are certain polities differing from one another, so it is also with souls. For they too have places from which they set out, and the soul that has set out from the more glorious place is nobler than one not so circumstanced. For just as among human beings the free man is held to be nobler than the slave—since that which is superior and kingly in souls of necessity enslaves that which is inferior—so indeed, my child, also * * *
— Do souls come to be male and female?
How souls come to be male and female.

— Souls, my child Horus, are of one nature with one another, inasmuch as they are from one region, in which the craftsman shaped them, and they are neither male nor female. For such a condition arises in bodies, and not in incorporeal things.

The difference by which some are fiercer and others soft lies in the air, my child Horus, in which all things come to be; and the air of a soul is the very body in which it is wrapped, which is a kneaded mass of elements, of earth and water and air and fire. Since, then, the compound of females has an excess of the moist and cold but falls short in the dry and hot, for this reason the soul shut up in such a moulded frame becomes moist through and through and delicate, just as in males one may find the opposite; for in them the dry and the hot are in excess, while the cold and moist are deficient, and for this reason the souls in such bodies are rough and more given to work.
— How do souls come to be discerning, mother?
— And Isis answered:
How souls come to be discerning.

The organ of sight, my child, is wrapped in coats. When these coats are dense and thick, the eye sees dimly; but if they are rare and fine, then it sees most keenly. So it is with the soul also; for it too has coverings of its own, incorporeal, inasmuch as it is itself incorporeal. And these coverings are of the air that is in us. When they are fine and rare and transparent, then the soul is discerning; but when, on the contrary, they are dense and thick and turbid, then, as in stormy weather, it does not see far, but only those things that lie at its feet.
— And Horus said: For what reason then, mother, are the people outside our most holy land not so discerning in their thought as our own people?

— And Isis said: The earth lies in the middle of the universe on its back, like a human being, looking towards heaven. And it is divided into as many parts as a human being is divided into; and it gazes into heaven as upon its own father, so that with the changes of heaven it too may change what is its own. It has its head lying towards the south of the universe, its right shoulder towards the east, its feet beneath the Bear, the left beneath the head of the Bear, its thighs in the regions that come after the Bear, and its middle parts in the middle regions.

And a sign of this is that those of humankind who are southern and dwell upon the crown of the head have well-formed heads and fine hair; that the easterners are ready for battle and are archers, for the right hand is the cause of this in them; that those in the west are steady and for the most part fight left-handed, and whatever others perform with the right side, they do by applying the left; and that those beneath the Bear are in some respect distinguished in their feet, and have well-formed legs besides. As for those who come after these and a little farther off, the clime that is now the Italian and the Greek, all these have fine thighs and are more amply bearded, so that through the surpassing beauty of these parts the people there even descend to intercourse with males.

Now all these parts, being sluggish in every other respect, have also produced the people who come from them more sluggish. But since the most holy land of our ancestors lies in the middle of the earth, and the middle of the human body is the sanctuary of the heart alone, and the heart is the soul’s base of operations, for this reason, my child, the people here, while they have all other things no less than all the rest, are as a special distinction more gifted in mind than all and are temperate, as having been born and reared upon the heart.

Moreover, the south, my child, being receptive of the clouds that are formed out of the encompassing atmosphere (for instance, it is because the clouds thus produced are carried down there that our own river also is said to flow from that quarter, the frost being melted there)—and wherever a cloud descends, it darkens the air beneath it with mist and fills it, in a manner, with smoke; and smoke or mist is a hindrance not only to the eyes but also to the mind. The east, Horus of great renown, being disturbed and heated through by the nearness of the sun’s rising, and likewise the west that lies opposite to it, sharing the same conditions at the sun’s setting, produce no clear attentiveness in the people born in them; and the north, by its inborn cold, congeals along with their bodies the mind also of the people beneath it.

But the middle of these, being clear and undisturbed, excels both in itself and in all who are in it; for by its unbroken freedom from care it begets and adorns and educates; and it alone contends with so many and prevails, and, knowing its own victory, like a good satrap it even bestows gifts upon the vanquished.
— Set this also before me, lady mother: for what reason, while people are still alive, in long illnesses their speech and their very reasoning and their very soul are sometimes impaired.

— And Isis answered: Of living beings, my child, some have an affinity with fire, some with water, some with air, some with earth, some with two or three of these, and some with them all; and again, some are estranged from fire, some from water, some from earth, some from air, some from two of these, some from three, and some from all.

For example, the locust, my child, and every fly shuns fire; the eagle and the falcon and all the higher-flying birds shun water; fish shun air and earth; the snake turns away from pure air. On the other hand, snakes and all creeping things love earth; all things that move love water; winged things love air, in which they also pass their lives; and fire is loved by all that fly exceedingly high and have their dwelling near it. What is more, some animals too love fire, such as salamanders; for they even make their lairs in fire.

For each of the elements is a wrapping of bodies. Every soul, therefore, while it is in the body, is weighed down and oppressed by these four. And indeed it is likely that the soul too takes delight in some of them and is vexed by others. For this reason, then, it does not have here its highest happiness, but, as being divine by nature, even while it is among these it struggles; and it thinks, but not all that it would have thought were it not bound to a body. If, however, the body too is seized by tossing and disturbance, whether from disease or from fear, then the soul itself, like a human being in the deep, is tossed upon the waves, and is swept along offering no resistance.
Excerpt XXV · Hermes: a discourse of Isis to Horus

Wonderfully, said Horus, have you related each thing to me, Isis, my mother of great power, concerning God’s wonderful making of souls, and I continue in wonder; but you have not yet reported to me where souls go when they have been released from bodies. I wish, therefore, when I have become an initiate of this doctrine also, to give thanks to you alone, immortal mother.
— And Isis said: Give heed, my child; for this inquiry is most necessary. That which holds together and does not vanish has a place.
But this is what my account will say.
Where souls abide when they have been released from bodies.

For it is not the case, wondrous one, great child of the great father Osiris, that when they have come forth from bodies they are poured out into the air without distinction and in a rush, and scattered along with the rest of the boundless breath, and are then no longer able to run back again into bodies as the same souls, nor yet able any longer to return to that place from which they came at first—just as it is not possible either for the water taken from the vessels below to be poured back into the same places from which it was taken, nor does the water itself, the moment it is taken and poured out, receive its own proper place, but it is mingled with the whole mass of water.

But it is not so, high-minded Horus. Being myself, as it were, an initiate of the immortal nature, and having journeyed through the plain of truth, I will go through for you the things that are, each in detail, telling you this first: that water is an irrational body, compounded out of many things pressed together into a fluid, whereas the soul is a thing of a nature all its own, my child, and kingly, and a work of the hands and mind of God, guided by its own self towards mind. Now that which is from one and not from many cannot be mingled with another thing; hence its coming together with the body also, a harmony of God, must have come about under necessity.

And that souls are sent up neither to one and the same place in a confused mass, nor at random and haphazardly, but each to its own proper region, is evident even from what the soul undergoes while it is still in the body and the moulded frame; for it suffers, having been made gross contrary to its own nature.

But attend also, much longed-for Horus, to the comparison I am about to give. Suppose that there have been shut up in one and the same enclosure human beings, and eagles and doves and swans and hawks and swallows and sparrows and flies, and snakes, and lions and leopards and wolves and dogs and hares and oxen and sheep, and some of the animals that share in both ways of life, such as seals and otters and turtles and our own crocodiles; and then, my child, that they are released from the enclosure at one single moment.

Will not the human beings assuredly turn to market-places and houses, the eagle to the aether, where it is its nature to live, the doves to the air nearby, and the hawks above these? Will not the swallows go wherever human beings dwell, the sparrows about the fruit-bearing trees, the swans where they are free to sing, and the flies about the earth itself, keeping as far from it as they are able to rise on the scent of human beings? For the fly, my child, is in a special way greedy for human beings, and keeps low to the ground. Will not the lions and leopards go to the mountains, the wolves to the wilds, the dogs on the track of human beings, the hares to the thickets, the oxen to steadings and plains, and the flocks to the pastures? And the snakes into the recesses of the earth? And the seals and turtles, with their like, into deep waters and streams, so that they may neither be deprived of level ground nor be left without their kindred water, each being turned back to its own proper region by the power of judgement within it?

So each soul, both that which lives as a human being and that which otherwise dwells upon earth, knows where it must go—unless indeed one of Typhon’s brood, my child, should come forward and say that it is possible for a bull to live out its life in the deep and a turtle in the air. If, then, souls are so affected while immersed in flesh and blood, so as to do nothing contrary to order even though they are being punished—for embodiment is a punishment for them—how much more when they have had their share of immersion and punishment and have come into their own freedom?

The most holy arrangement is as follows. Now at last, my child of noblest nature, look upward and behold the arrangements of souls. The space from the summit of heaven down to the moon is set apart for gods and stars and the rest of providence; but the space from the moon down to us, my child, is the dwelling-place of souls.

This great expanse of air, however, which it is our custom to call wind, has within itself a path, an extent of its own in which it moves for the refreshing of the things on earth; of this too I will speak later. Yet in no way does it, in moving upon itself, become a hindrance to souls; for while it is in motion souls are free to dart up and to dart down, as it may chance, without obstruction. For they flow through it without mingling and without adhering, as water through oil.

This interval, my child Horus, consists of four general divisions and of sixty particular regions. Of these divisions, the one that extends upward from the earth consists of four regions, so that the earth, in certain hills and mountain ridges, stretches up and reaches thus far; for above this division it is not in its nature to rise in height. The second after this consists of eight regions, in which the movements of winds take place. Give heed, my child; for you are hearing ineffable mysteries of earth and of heaven and of all the holy breath between. Where the movement of the wind is, there too is the flight of birds; for above this division neither does the air move nor does it bear up a living being. This air, however, has from nature this prerogative, that it ranges about both in its own eight regions and in the four of the earth, together with the living beings that it holds, whereas the earth is not able to mount up into the regions of the air.

The third consists of sixteen regions, and is full of fine and pure air. The fourth consists of thirty-two, in which the air is finest and most unmixed and transparent, marking off at its own boundary the heavens above, which are fiery by nature.

And this arrangement runs in a straight line from above downward, by nature without adhesion, so that there are four general divisions, twelve divisions by interval, and sixty regions. In these regions, sixty in number, the souls dwell, each according to the nature that it has, being of one and the same constitution but not, however, of the same honour; for by as much as each of the regions surpasses another in distance from the earth, by so much also, among the souls in them, does one leave another behind in eminence, my child: region and soul alike.
Which souls, then, depart to each of these regions I will now begin again to recount to you from this point, Horus of great renown, taking the order from above down to the parts near the earth.
Excerpt XXVI

The space between earth and heaven has been divided into regions, my child Horus, according to measure and harmony. These regions are called by our ancestors, by some ‘zones’, by others ‘firmaments’, and by others again ‘folds’. In them move to and fro both the souls that have been released from bodies and those that have not yet been embodied. And each of these, my child, has a region too according to its dignity, so that the divine and kingly souls dwell in the region above all the rest, while those that are least in honour, and all the others that keep low to the ground, dwell in the region beneath all the rest, and the middle souls in the middle region.

Now the souls that are sent down to rule, my child Horus, are sent down from the upper zones; and when they are released they go up to the same zones or even higher still, unless some of them should yet have acted against the dignity of their own nature and the injunction of the divine law; for these the providence above banishes to the lower regions in the measure of their sins, just as it also leads up those that are inferior in power and dignity from lower regions to greater and higher ones.

For there are on high those who are the bodyguards of universal providence, of whom one is the steward of souls and the other the conductor of souls; and the steward of souls has charge of souls, while the conductor of souls is the dispatcher and marshal of the souls that are being embodied; and the one keeps them, the other sends them forth, according to the will of God.

By this account, then, my child, and in keeping with the diversity of things above, nature too is upon earth, for she is a moulder, and a tent-maker of the vessels into which the souls are cast. And two energies stand beside her also, memory and skill. Memory has this as its work, that nature may preserve and hold fast to each type laid down from the beginning, and may keep to the pattern above; and skill has this, that the moulded frame too may be wrought and come to be in proportion to each of the souls that descend to be embodied, and that for the quick among souls the bodies too may turn out quick, for the slow slow, for the active active, for the sluggish sluggish, for the powerful powerful, for the crafty crafty, and in a word for each as is fitting.

For it was not without aim that she feathered the winged creatures, and adorned the rational ones with senses superior and more exact, and of the four-footed strengthened some with horns, some with teeth, some with claws and hooves. The creeping things she made soft, with supple and yielding bodies; and so that they might not remain utterly weak through the moistness of their body, she palisaded the mouths of some with teeth, and upon others, by increasing their bulk, she bestowed power. Thus these, through wariness of death, are stronger than the rest; while to the swimming creatures, being timid, she granted to dwell in an element in which light has strength to exert neither of the powers it possesses; for in water fire neither shines nor burns; and each of them, swimming in the water with scales or with spines, flees wherever it will, wrapped in its own timidity and having the water as a covering so that it is not seen.

For into each of these bodies the souls are shut up according to likeness, so that into human beings go the souls endowed with judgement; into winged creatures those that shun humankind; into four-footed creatures those without judgement, for among them strength is law; into creeping things the crafty, for none of them comes against human beings face to face, but lies in ambush and strikes them down; and into the swimming creatures the timid, and all that are unworthy to enjoy the other elements.
It does happen, however, that in each kind one finds a living being that does not make use of its own nature.
— How so again, mother? said Horus.

— And Isis answered: In such a way, my child, that a human being oversteps the faculty of judgement, a four-footed creature turns aside from necessity, a creeping thing loses its craftiness, a swimming creature scorns its timidity, and a winged creature falls away from its shunning of humankind.
So much, then, concerning the disposition of the things above, their descent, and the making of bodies.

It comes about, my child, that in each form and kind of the creatures in question certain kingly souls are found, and that others too come down of differing sorts, some fiery, some cold, some haughty, some gentle, some of the artisan’s kind, some skilled, some unskilled, some idle, some active, and some differing in some other way. This comes about by reason of the position of the places from which the souls leap down to be embodied. For some leap down from a kingly belt, the soul that reigns being of like affection with it.
For there are many kingships: some are of souls, some of bodies, some of art, some of science, and some of themselves.
— How again, said Horus, ‘of themselves’ also?

— For example, my child Horus, of the souls of those already departed Osiris your father is king; of bodies, the leader of each nation; of counsel, the father of all and guide, Hermes Trismegistus; of medicine, Asclepius the son of Hephaestus; of might and strength, again Osiris, and after him, my child, you yourself; of philosophy, Harnebeschenis; of poetry, again Asclepius Imouthes. For in general, my child, you will find, if you inquire, many who rule over many things and many who reign over many.

But he who holds sway over all, my child, is from the uppermost region, while he who holds sway over particular things has received that more kingly rank which belongs to the place from which he comes.

* * * belt for their lot, become workers of fire and of nourishment; those from a moist belt pass their lives in what is moist; those from a belt of science and art are occupied with sciences and arts; those from an idle belt live out their lives idly and aimlessly. For of all the things on earth, my child, that are done through word and deed, the sources are above, pouring their essences upon us by measure and weight, and there is nothing that has not come down from above.
And it goes up again to the place from which it came down.
— How do you mean this again, mother? Show me by an example.

— And Isis answered again: Most holy nature has set in living beings this clear sign of the return. For this breath which we draw from above out of the air, this we send up again to the place from which we took it. And there are in us, my child, bellows that are the artisans of this working; and when these have closed their mouths that receive the breath, then we are no longer here, but have ascended.
There come to us in addition, my child of great renown, certain other things from the balance of the kneaded mass.
— And what is this kneaded mass, mother? said Horus.

— It is a coming together and blending of the four elements, and from this blending and coming together a certain vapour is exhaled, which wraps itself around the soul and runs through the body, imparting to both, that is to the body and to the soul, something of its own quality; and in this way arise the differences in the alterations of soul and of body.

For if in the framing of the body fire is in excess, then the soul, being hot by nature and having taken on a further heat, becomes more fiery and makes the living being more active and spirited, and the body quick and nimble.
If air is in excess, then the living being becomes light and given to leaping and unsteady, both in soul and in body.

If water is in excess, then the living being becomes in soul easy-flowing and of good natural gifts and ready to spread itself around, and well able to fall in with others and cleave to them, because of the uniting and sociable character of water towards other things; for it settles upon all things, and when it is much it dissolves them into itself and encloses them, while when it is little and has sunk in, it becomes that with which it was mixed. The bodies, however, by reason of their flabbiness and sponginess are not drawn together into compactness, but at some slight occasion of disease they come apart, and little by little fall away from their own bond.

If the earthy element is in excess, then the soul of the living being becomes dull, since it does not have the looseness of the body’s texture lying open to it, nor anything through which it may leap forth, the organs of sense having been thickened; rather it remains within, by itself, fettered by weight and density; and the body is solid, but sluggish and heavy, and is shifted by the will only with an effort.
But if the state of all the elements is well proportioned, then the living being is constituted hot for action, light for movement, well tempered for touch, and sturdy in its solidity.

According to this account, then, all those that have partaken of more fire and breath have been made into birds, and they have their life as citizens above, among those elements from which they also came to be.

Those that have partaken of more fire, but of little breath, and of water and earth in equal measure, have been made into human beings; and for this living being the surplus of heat has been turned into understanding. For the mind in us is a hot thing, which does not know how to burn, but penetrates through all things and has knowledge of them.

Those that have partaken of more water and of more earth, of a moderate measure of breath and of little fire, have been made into beasts; and by the presence of heat they have become more valiant than the others.

Those that have partaken of earth and water in equal amounts have been made into creeping things; and by the lack of fire they have become without daring and without openness, by their share in water they became cold, by their share in earth heavy and sluggish, and by their share in breath easily moved, if they choose to move.

Those that have partaken of more of the moist and of little of the dry have been made into fish; and by the lack of heat and of air they are timid and given to diving down, while by the abundance of the moist and the presence of the earthy they dwell, through kinship, in dissolved earth and in water.

And in proportion to the share of each element and the extent of that share the bodies also grow to their stature, and in proportion to smallness of measure the remaining living beings have received their measure, according to the energy of the measure of essence that belongs to each of the elements.

And I say further, my much longed-for child, that, arising from this constitution so formed, the blending that took place at the first coming together and the vapour exhaled from it, so long as it keeps its own quality, so that the hot takes on no further heat, nor the airy element further breath, nor the moist further moisture, nor the earthy further density, so long the living being is in health. For whenever it does not remain thus, my child, in the measures which it had from the beginning, but comes to exceed them—I do not mean in the energy that concerns extent, nor in that change of the kind and of the bodies which comes about through growth, but in the constitutive blending of the elements of which we spoke before—so that the hot is increased too much or diminished too much, and the others likewise, then the living being is thereby sick.

For when the hot and the airy, which are the tent-fellows of the soul, are in this condition, then the living being falls into wandering speech and fits of derangement. For the elements through which bodies are destroyed have been made dense.

For the earthy element is itself the solidity of the body, the moist is the suffusion within it that makes for compactness, the airy is that in us which gives movement, and fire is what rouses all of these.

So then the vapour that arises from the first coming together and blending of the elements, being as it were a kindling and an exhalation, of whatever kind it may be, when it is mingled with the soul draws the soul to itself, according to whatever nature it has, whether good or not.

For so long as the soul abides in its original kinship and companionship with the vapour, it preserves its order; but when there is added from without, either to the whole compound or to parts or a part of it, some portion greater than what was laid down at first, then the vapour too, being altered thereby, alters either the disposition of the soul or that of the body.
For fire and breath, being borne upward, run up to the soul, which shares their region, while the moist and the earthy, being borne downward, settle upon the body, which shares their seat.

Thales, when asked what is the oldest of the things that are, answered: ‘God, for he is unbegotten.’
Socrates, when asked what God is, said: ‘That which is immortal and eternal.’

Excerpt XXIX · Of Hermes

Seven far-wandering stars circle upon the threshold of Olympus, and with them the aeon for ever goes its round: the Moon who shines by night, sullen Cronus, the sweet Sun, the Paphian who bears the bridal bower, bold Ares, well-winged Hermes, and Zeus, first author of birth, from whom nature has sprung. These same have had the race of mortals allotted to them, and there are in us. Moon, Zeus, Ares, the Paphian, Kronos, Sun, Hermes. Therefore it is our portion to draw from the aetherial breath. tears, laughter, wrath, birth, reason, sleep, desire. Tears are Kronos, Zeus is birth, reason is Hermes, anger is Ares, the Moon is sleep, Cytherea is desire, and the Sun is laughter; for through him, rightly, all mortal thought laughs, and the boundless cosmos too.
